title: YOU THOUGHT GOD FORGOT YOU: THE HEARTBREAKING TRUTH BEHIND ISAIAH 40:31
paragraphs: YOU THOUGHT GOD FORGOT YOU: THE HEARTBREAKING TRUTH BEHIND ISAIAH 40:31
What “Wait Upon the Lord” Really Means When You Have Prayed, Cried, Believed—and Nothing Seems to Be Changing
There is a kind of waiting that feels almost cruel.
Not waiting for your coffee.
Not waiting for traffic to move.
Not waiting for someone to answer a message.
I mean the kind of waiting where you have prayed until you no longer know what to say.
The kind where you wake up and the situation is still there.
The diagnosis has not changed.
The marriage is still strained.
The child is still far from God.
The door is still closed.
The loneliness is still sitting beside you.
The temptation you thought you would have conquered by now still knows your name.
The grief still ambushes you in ordinary places.
The financial pressure still follows you to bed.
And perhaps the hardest part is this:
God could change it.
You know He could.
So why hasn't He?
That is where Isaiah 40:31 is often quoted.
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength…”
Beautiful words.
But when your heart is exhausted, beautiful words can become painful words if nobody explains what they actually mean.
Because maybe you have waited.
And waited.
And waited.
And instead of feeling stronger, you feel tired.
So tired that you have quietly wondered whether this promise works for everybody except you.
If that is where you are, Isaiah 40 was written for people who understood that feeling far more deeply than we sometimes realize.
And the verse becomes even more powerful when we stop treating it like an inspirational slogan and listen to what God was actually saying.
Isaiah 40:31 reads in Hebrew:

וְקוֹיֵי יְהוָה יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ
יַעֲלוּ אֵבֶר כַּנְּשָׁרִים
יָרוּצוּ וְלֹא יִיגָעוּ
יֵלְכוּ וְלֹא יִיעָפוּ
Wəqōwê YHWH yaḥălîp̄û kōaḥ; yaʿălû ʾēḇer kannəšārîm; yārûṣû wəlō yîgāʿû; yēlḵû wəlō yîʿāp̄û.
The familiar King James rendering says:
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.”
But here is what changes everything.
Biblical waiting is not doing nothing.
And waiting upon the Lord does not mean pretending you are not hurting while you passively sit around hoping something eventually happens.
The Hebrew expression translated “they that wait upon the LORD” comes from the verb קָוָה — qāvâ.
In this context, it carries the sense of waiting with hope, looking expectantly toward someone, trusting and hoping in the one upon whom your expectation rests.
That distinction matters.
You are not merely waiting for something.
You are waiting upon Someone.
That means Isaiah 40:31 is not primarily a promise about God giving impatient people faster circumstances.
It is about God becoming the inexhaustible source of strength for people whose own strength has reached its end.
And maybe that is exactly where God has found you.
At the end of yourself.
You thought reaching the end of yourself meant you had failed.
God may be showing you that you have finally discovered where His strength begins to become unmistakable.
Look at the heartbreaking question immediately before the famous promise.
Isaiah 40:27 says:
“Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God?”
There it is.
The Bible does not sanitize the feeling.
God's people were essentially saying:
God doesn't see me.
My situation has escaped His attention.
My cause has been overlooked.
Sound familiar?
You prayed.
Nothing happened.
You obeyed.
The door remained closed.
You tried to live faithfully while someone who seemingly cared nothing about God appeared to prosper.
You watched other people announce the engagement, the pregnancy, the healing, the breakthrough, the ministry opportunity, the restored relationship.
You congratulated them.
You smiled.
You even thanked God for blessing them.
Then you put your phone down.
And something inside you whispered:
“Lord… what about me?”
That whisper is closer to Isaiah 40 than many polished sermons ever get.
God does not answer Israel by humiliating them for being tired.
He answers by reminding exhausted people who He is.
“Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?”
Isaiah 40:28.
Read that slowly.
You become weary.
God does not.
You lose perspective.
God does not.
You cannot see tomorrow.
God already stands sovereign over it.
Your emotional resources can collapse.
His character cannot.
Your body can become exhausted.
His power cannot.
Your plans can fall apart.
His throne does not.
That is why verse 29 says:
“He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.”
Notice who receives strength.
The faint.
The powerless.
The person who finally has to admit:
“I cannot carry this anymore.”
Christianity was never the story of impressive people proving how strong they are for God.
The Gospel is the story of helpless sinners being rescued by a mighty Savior.
That pattern reaches its blazing center in Jesus Christ.
Humanity could not climb its way back to God.
Religion could not erase our guilt.
Good intentions could not remove sin.
Self-improvement could not reconcile rebels to a holy God.
So Christ came to us.
Jesus lived the righteousness we could not produce.
He bore sin at the cross.
He entered death.
And He rose victorious.
The scandal of human sin met the greater scandal of divine grace.
The guilty could be forgiven.
The condemned could be justified.
The runaway could come home.
The ashamed could be clothed in Christ's righteousness.
The spiritually dead could receive life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And that changes how Christians wait.
We do not wait wondering whether God loves us.
The cross has already answered that question.
We do not wait wondering whether sin gets the final word.
The empty tomb has already answered that question.
We do not wait because God has abandoned His throne.
We wait because the God who cannot become weary is still God when we are completely exhausted.
Then Isaiah says something remarkable:
“Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall.”
Even youth fails.
Even natural strength fails.
Even the person everyone assumes can handle everything eventually discovers a limit.
Your limit is not God's limit.
Then comes the promise:
וְקוֹיֵי יְהוָה יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ
Wəqōwê YHWH yaḥălîp̄û kōaḥ.
Those who wait for—hope in—the LORD “shall renew their strength.”
The verb translated “renew” is related to חָלַף — ḥālap̄, carrying ideas such as changing, passing on, replacing, or renewing depending on context.
The picture is not that exhausted believers somehow manufacture another reserve of human determination.
Their hope rests in the God who “giveth power to the faint.”
That destroys one of the most dangerous lies exhausted Christians believe:
“I just need to try harder.”
Sometimes you don't.
Sometimes you need to stop pretending your strength is infinite.
You need God.
Not merely another productivity system.
Not another motivational speech.
Not another mask.
God.
Maybe your waiting season has exposed things you did not know were inside you.
Control.
Fear.
Bitterness.
Jealousy.
Secret sin.
An addiction to people's approval.
Anger toward God.
A relationship you made into an idol.
A dream you began loving more than the One who gave you the ability to dream.
Waiting has a strange way of revealing what comfort allowed us to hide.
When God does not immediately give us what we want, we sometimes discover whether we wanted God—or merely wanted God to give us something.
That realization can hurt.
But conviction is not the same thing as rejection.
Jesus exposes wounds in order to heal.
He confronts sin in order to call sinners into repentance and grace.
So perhaps the deepest question of your waiting season is not merely:
“When will God change this?”
Perhaps another question needs to be asked:
“What is God doing in me while I am waiting?”
Because sometimes we become so obsessed with escaping the waiting room that we miss the Savior sitting with us inside it.
Isaiah continues:
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary…”
Those are the lines everybody remembers.
Flying.
Running.
Strength.
Victory.
But then comes the final phrase.
“And they shall walk, and not faint.”
Walk?
After soaring?
After running?
Why end there?
Perhaps because much of faithfulness does not look like soaring.
It looks like walking.
Getting out of bed when your heart is heavy.
Opening Scripture when you feel spiritually dry.
Praying when you cannot feel anything spectacular.
Refusing the temptation you secretly want.
Forgiving again.
Repenting again.
Showing up again.
Choosing truth again.
Taking another ordinary step with Jesus.
We love testimonies about soaring because soaring looks miraculous.
But sometimes the miracle is that you are still walking.
Nobody applauded.
Nobody posted about it.
Nobody knew how close you came to giving up.
But you woke up.
And somehow whispered:
“Jesus, I still trust You.”
Then you took another step.
That is not insignificant faith.
Sometimes that is faith stripped down to its purest form.
Maybe you expected God to make you fly over the valley.
Instead, He is giving you enough grace to walk through it.
Do not despise that grace.
The Lord who gives strength for soaring is also the Lord who gives strength for the next step.
And Scripture never promises that waiting upon God means every earthly story will resolve exactly as we demand.
Some prayers are answered differently than we hoped.
Some doors remain closed.
Some losses are not reversed in this life.
Some faithful believers die still waiting for things they longed to see.
Christian hope therefore cannot ultimately rest in getting the earthly ending we wrote for ourselves.
Our hope rests in Christ.
Romans 8 points believers beyond present suffering toward coming glory.
Revelation 21 points toward the day when God will wipe away every tear and death will be no more.
The Christian does not merely believe:
“Eventually everything will happen exactly the way I want.”
The Christian believes something far stronger:
“Whatever happens, Jesus Christ will remain faithful, and because I belong to Him, suffering, sin, death, and the grave will not have the final word.”
That is hope sturdy enough for a hospital room.
A cemetery.
A divorce court.
A rejection letter.
An empty bank account.
A prodigal child's bedroom.
A sleepless night.
A season where heaven seems silent.
Maybe God has not forgotten you.
Maybe silence is not absence.
Maybe waiting is not rejection.
Maybe the chapter you called “God abandoned me” will someday look completely different from the other side of eternity.
But there is also something you must not miss.
Waiting upon the Lord is not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
If the thing exhausting your soul is rebellion against God, the biblical response is not merely to “wait for strength.”
Repent.
Come into the light.
Bring the hidden thing to Jesus.
Stop negotiating with what Christ died to free you from.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace cost the blood of Christ.
And the same Savior who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
If you have wandered far from God, you do not need to clean yourself up enough to earn your journey home.
Come home.
If you have fallen again, confess it.
If shame tells you to hide, remember what happened in Eden: sin drove humanity into hiding.
But the Gospel announces that God came looking for sinners.
Jesus still saves sinners.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still transforms.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years believing that what happened in your worst chapter permanently became your identity.
It didn't.
Your scandal does not outrank His grace.
Your failure is not more powerful than His cross.
Your past is not sovereign.
Jesus is.
Peter had denial in his story.
Paul had persecution in his story.
The woman at the well had brokenness in hers.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes.
Yet grace entered their stories.
That does not make sin beautiful.
It makes the Savior magnificent.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So what does it mean to wait upon the Lord?
It means your expectation shifts from your own strength to His faithfulness.
It means you keep trusting when immediate evidence does not give you everything you want.
It means praying without treating God like a vending machine.
It means obeying when obedience costs you.
It means repenting when waiting exposes sin.
It means remembering who God is when circumstances tempt you to rewrite His character.
It means believing that the everlasting Creator has not become exhausted by your need.
It means allowing your weakness to drive you toward Christ instead of deeper into hiding.
And sometimes…
it simply means walking.
One more prayer.
One more act of obedience.
One more confession.
One more morning.
One more “Jesus, help me.”
One more step.
If you are reading this while spiritually exhausted, you do not have to pretend here.
Be honest.
Not because a comment is a magic formula.
Not because typing words earns God's favor.
But because sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is the first time we stop pretending we are okay.
And if God has used this to expose something you need to surrender, you can simply write:
Let somebody else reading the comments discover they are not the only Christian who has struggled.
Let testimony become community.
Let honesty point people toward grace.
Not as a religious performance.
Not to prove you are spiritual.
Send it privately to the family member whose faith has been bruised.

Do not leave Jesus outside your waiting.
Bring Him your exhaustion.
Bring Him the prayer you stopped praying.
Bring Him the anger you were afraid to admit.
Bring Him your secret sin.
Bring Him the disappointment.
Bring Him the dream.
Bring Him the diagnosis.
Bring Him the relationship.
Bring Him the future you cannot control.
Bring Him the part of your story you are convinced cannot possibly be redeemed.
And wait upon the Lord.
Not because waiting guarantees that tomorrow will look exactly the way you wanted.
But because the One you are waiting upon is everlasting.
He does not faint.
He does not grow weary.
His understanding is unsearchable.
He gives power to the faint.
And in Jesus Christ, even death itself does not get the final sentence.
Perhaps you are not soaring today.
Perhaps you are not running.
Perhaps all you can do is walk.
Then walk.
And if all you can manage right now is one trembling step toward Jesus…
take it.
Because one day you may discover that the season in which you thought God was doing nothing was the very season in which He was teaching your exhausted heart where strength had always come from.
You thought you were waiting for God to change your circumstances—but perhaps, in the silence, Christ was refusing to let your circumstances become your god.
